title: Proof pages for a nonprofit
metaTitle: What a nonprofit case study should show
excerpt: Show the constraint, the decision, and the work in the world, with consent intact. Close by telling a similar reader how to give, join, or read the program.
alt: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase arranged on a white shelf, for a piece on showing the work itself, not a mood.
caption: Objects on a shelf, specific and still. A proof should be this concrete. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What makes a nonprofit proof different from an appeal?
faqs.answer: A proof shows judgment. The constraint, the option you did not take, and what changed in the world. An appeal asks for a feeling and a gift. The proof can end with a gift or an application, but the story has to stand without the ask.

faqs.question: How should participants appear?
faqs.answer: Only with consent you would show a board, and never as a requirement for receiving help. If a story cannot be told without exposing someone, tell the decision and the system instead. Do not invent a composite quote and put a name-like label on it.

faqs.question: When should a proof come down?
faqs.answer: When the program has changed so the story would mislead. If the added night no longer exists, update the page or remove it. Date the work and review the set when you review the annual report. Expired miracles train readers to discount the next page.

markdown:
A nonprofit case study page is a record of a real constraint, a real decision, and the work in the world. A donor or a participant deciding whether the work is real does not need a highlight reel. They need to see what was hard, what you chose, and what changed for a person or a place. Screenshots of a gala and pull quotes with no decision are decoration. The page should end by showing a similar reader how to give, join, or read the program.

Write it so someone who was not in the room can audit the story. If a sentence would embarrass you in front of a participant who lived it, it does not belong. If a number would embarrass you in front of your bookkeeper, it does not belong either.

## Open on the constraint

Name the bind in the first lines. A clinic list that outgrew the night. A trail washed out before the season's commitment was met. A pantry that had food and no way to get it to the second school. The constraint should be specific enough that a peer organization would nod, and plain enough that a donor would understand the stakes.

Keep the focus on the situation, not on the organization's heroism. The reader is trying to judge whether you can see a problem clearly. A clear problem is the start of trust. A dramatic prologue about a broken world, with the program arriving as the rescue, skips the seeing. Start with the operational fact.

Protect people in the telling. Change details that would identify a participant, and say that you have done so when it matters. Do not trade someone's privacy for a more vivid opening. A composite that pretends to be one person is a line you should not cross. If you cannot tell the story without exposing someone, tell a different story, about the system and the decision, and leave the portrait out.

Set the time and the place. Which season, which site. Undated miracles feel like marketing. Dated work feels like an organization that keeps records. You can still be brief. "Autumn 2024, the west side clinic" is a frame. The frame lets a reader decide whether this proof is a cousin of the situation they care about.

## The decision, including the option you declined

The center of the page is judgment. What you changed. What you refused to change. Why. Added a night. Narrowed eligibility so the people you could serve were served well. Stopped a partnership that looked good in a photo and failed in the room. Asked a funder to release a restriction that was bending the program out of shape.

Include a path you did not take. That is the signature of a real decision. You might have chased a second site and instead fixed the intake at the first. You might have bought more inventory and instead fixed the pickup hours that were the actual bottleneck. A donor who needs the work to be real is looking for evidence that someone weighed tradeoffs. A list of activities does not show a tradeoff.

Name the role that decided. The program lead, the board, the members at a meeting. Shared decisions can be described as shared. Unowned decisions feel written by a communications volunteer after the fact, because they often were. If you are writing after the fact, sit with the person who decided and use their reason, not a prettier one.

Keep the detail at a human scale. One change, one reason, one consequence. A proof page that retells the entire strategic plan will lose the participant who wanted to know if your intake is sane, and it will lose the donor who wanted to know if you can focus. Link the program page for the standing offer. Keep this page on the one hard thing.

## The work in the world

Show what was different afterward, in the world rather than in your feelings. More people seen on the added night. The segment cleared by the date you had promised the land partner. The second school receiving bags on a day families could actually carry them home. The result should be observable.

Use a number only when you can point to the sheet it came from. Attendance, meals, cases closed, dollars spent on the program. Define the unit in the sentence. "Forty households picked up that month" is a fact. "Impact soared" is a mood. If the honest result was mixed, say so. A partial result that you understand is more persuasive than a total victory that sounds drafted for a newsletter.

Photographs from the work need consent and need to show the decision. The added room, the revised route, the pickup at the second school. A smiling crowd with no relation to the constraint is the decoration you are trying to retire. If photography would expose participants, use the place, the materials, and the schedule, and let the writing hold the human stake.

Credit partners without inflating them, and without hiding them. If the school made the second pickup possible, say what the school did. A proof that claims solo credit for a shared effort will be read by the partner. Write the sentence you can send them before you publish.

## Consent, credit, and what you will not show

Write a small rule for the organization and follow it on every proof. Participants are not required to appear. Staff appear when they agree. Minors appear only under the policy your board would defend. Locations that would put someone at risk are generalized. You can publish a strong page inside those rules. The rules are what make the page something you can stand next to.

Quotes follow the same rule. A person's words, with permission, in context, about the constraint. No tidying that changes the meaning. No quote you wrote and attributed to "a mom." If you do not have permission, paraphrase the situation without a puppet voice. Readers can tell when a quote is doing advertising. The tell is smoothness. Real remarks have edges. Keep the edges or do not use the remark.

Thank funders by telling the truth about what the money did. "This season's added night was funded by X" is a credit. "We are grateful to our incredible partners" is a toast. The credit belongs in the proof because it shows how the work is paid for. The toast can happen in the room.

[Google's helpful-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks for first-hand experience and for pages that leave someone clearer. A proof meets that bar when the constraint was lived, the decision has an owner, and a reader knows what they can do next. It misses when the page could have been assembled from last year's appeal and a stock photo.

## Close with a similar reader's next step

The last block is for the person who recognized themselves or their gift. Tell them how to enter. Join, if the program in the story is open and they fit the boundary. Give, if the funding path that made the decision possible is still the path. Read the program, if they are not ready to do either and the standing offer is the honest next page.

Say who the proof is a good analogy for. "Relevant if you refer people who need a weeknight clinic." "Relevant if you fund capacity, not a one-day event." Also say who it is not for, in one line, so you do not attract applications you will have to refuse. The boundary is part of the craft. It continues the respect you showed in the story.

Use the same verbs as the rest of the site. A proof that ends with a unique long form, or with "learn more" into a void, drops the reader at the moment they were convinced. Match the contact path and the program block. One organization, one set of doors.

Link the report if the story's numbers live there. A reader who wants the table can go to the table. The proof stays narrative and checkable. It does not become an appendix. It does not become a press release with subheads about excitement.

## What does not belong

The gala as a substitute for the work. Award badges unrelated to the constraint. A video montage set to music, with the decision nowhere in the cut. Adjectives piled where a result should be. A participant's worst day, used as the hook. These are the habits of an appeal letter. A proof page has a different job. It shows judgment.

Do not publish a story the program lead would not walk through with a site visitor. The page will attract that conversation. If the answer to a likely question is "we cannot talk about that," narrow the story until the answer becomes "here is what we can say," and make sure what you can say is still a complete decision.

Do not keep a proof up after the program has changed in a way that makes the story misleading. If the added night no longer exists, update the page or take it down. A library of expired miracles trains donors to discount the next one. Date the work. Review the set when you review the annual report. The same season is a good rhythm.

## A small set, kept current

Three proofs that match the programs you want people to join or fund will beat a dozen thin posts. Choose constraints that show the range of your judgment. One about access. One about saying no. One about a partnership. If every proof is a triumph of growth, you have not shown that you can focus, and focus is what skeptical readers are shopping for.

On a Hanabi project, a proof is a page in the same system as the program and the homepage, with the same action at the end and a folder in the client portal for permissions, drafts, and the source for every number. The studio designs and builds the page. You decide what may be shown. That line should stay bright.

See how a public site handles a specific story by looking at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The parallel is discipline. A visitor can tell what was done and why it mattered, without a private tour.

After a proof, the reader still has to move around the site without learning your departments. [Navigation for a nonprofit](/blog/navigation-for-a-nonprofit) is the next piece, because the menu should be a map of jobs a donor or a participant already has words for, with one path to give, join, or read.
